side-01-c2.text: Paul C. Kocher (1996). Timing Attacks on Implementations of Diffie-Hellman, RSA, DSS, and Other Systems. Advances in Cryptology (CRYPTO '96), LNCS 1109, Springer.
side-01-c2.quote: By carefully measuring the amount of time required to perform private key operations, attackers may be able to find fixed Diffie-Hellman exponents, factor RSA keys, and break other cryptosystems.
side-01-c2.claim: The field as we know it began with a 1996 paper by Paul Kocher, Timing Attacks on Implementations of Diffie-Hellman, RSA, DSS, and Other Systems.

side-01-c2.text: Paul C. Kocher (1996). Timing Attacks on Implementations of Diffie-Hellman, RSA, DSS, and Other Systems. Advances in Cryptology (CRYPTO '96), LNCS 1109, Springer.
side-01-c2.quote: If it is zero, the operation will be skipped.
side-01-c2.claim: For each bit of the private exponent d, the algorithm always squares, but it only multiplies if the bit is 1.

side-02-c1.text: Daniel J. Bernstein (2005). Cache-timing attacks on AES. cr.yp.to (University of Illinois at Chicago).
side-02-c1.quote: This paper demonstrates complete AES key recovery from known-plaintext timings of a network server on another computer.
side-02-c1.claim: This was first practically demonstrated by Daniel J. Bernstein in 2005, attacking OpenSSL's AES across a network.

side-02-c1.text: Dag Arne Osvik, Adi Shamir, Eran Tromer (2005). Cache attacks and Countermeasures: the Case of AES. Cryptology ePrint Archive.
side-02-c1.quote: The attacks allow an unprivileged process to attack other processes running in parallel on the same processor, despite partitioning methods such as memory protection, sandboxing and virtualization.
side-02-c1.claim: Subsequent work by Osvik, Shamir, and Tromer (2006) showed full AES-128 key recovery in seconds with co-resident attackers.

side-02-c2.text: Yuval Yarom, Katrina Falkner (2014). FLUSH+RELOAD: A High Resolution, Low Noise, L3 Cache Side-Channel Attack. 23rd USENIX Security Symposium.
side-02-c2.quote: We demonstrate the efficacy of the FLUSH+RELOAD attack by using it to extract the private encryption keys from a victim program running GnuPG 1.4.13.
side-02-c2.claim: Yarom and Falkner (2014) used Flush+Reload to extract a full GnuPG private key from a co-resident victim: sub-millisecond per cache observation, full key in minutes.

side-02-c3.text: Oscar Reparaz, Josep Balasch, Ingrid Verbauwhede (2016). Dude, is my code constant time?. Cryptology ePrint Archive.
side-02-c3.quote: This paper introduces dudect: a tool to assess whether a piece of code runs in constant time or not on a given platform.
side-02-c3.claim: The only way to be confident is to verify the binary: use tools like ctgrind, dudect, or formal verification (e.g., HACL*, Jasmin) that check timing leaks at the machine-code level.

side-03-c1.text: Paul Kocher, Joshua Jaffe, Benjamin Jun (1999). Differential Power Analysis. Advances in Cryptology: CRYPTO '99.
side-03-c1.quote: Simple Power Analysis (SPA) is a technique that involves directly interpreting power consumption measurements collected during cryptographic operations. SPA can yield information about a device's operation as well as key material.
side-03-c1.claim: Simple Power Analysis (SPA) reads the secret directly from a single trace.

side-03-c2.text: Paul Kocher, Joshua Jaffe, Benjamin Jun (1999). Differential Power Analysis. Advances in Cryptology: CRYPTO '99.
side-03-c2.quote: The leakage functions depend on the multiplier design, but are often strongly correlated to operand values and Hamming weights.
side-03-c2.claim: It only needs a power model, usually the Hamming weight (number of 1-bits) or Hamming distance (bits flipped) of an intermediate variable.

side-03-c3.text: Karine Gandolfi, Christophe Mourtel, Francis Olivier (2001). Electromagnetic Analysis: Concrete Results. Cryptographic Hardware and Embedded Systems (CHES 2001).
side-03-c3.quote: This work describes electromagnetic experiments conducted on three different cmos chips, featuring different hardware protections and executing a des, an alleged COMP128 and an RSA. In all cases the complete key material was successfully retrieved.
side-03-c3.claim: Quisquater and Samyde (2001) and Gandolfi, Mourtel, and Olivier (2001) demonstrated EM attacks recovering keys from smart cards through their plastic packaging.

side-03-c3.text: Daniel Genkin, Lev Pachmanov, Itamar Pipman, Eran Tromer (2016). ECDH Key-Extraction via Low-Bandwidth Electromagnetic Attacks on PCs. Tel Aviv University.
side-03-c3.quote: By measuring the target's electromagnetic emanations, the attack extracts the secret decryption key within seconds, from a target located in an adjacent room across a wall.
side-03-c3.claim: A 2016 follow-up by the same group extracted ECDH keys from an adjacent room, through a wall.

side-04-c2.text: Daniel Genkin, Adi Shamir, Eran Tromer (2013). RSA Key Extraction via Low-Bandwidth Acoustic Cryptanalysis. Tel Aviv University.
side-04-c2.quote: The attack can extract full 4096-bit RSA decryption keys from laptop computers (of various models), within an hour, using the sound generated by the computer during the decryption of some chosen ciphertexts.
side-04-c2.claim: With a parabolic microphone four meters away, or even an off-the-shelf smartphone resting on the laptop, the researchers extracted full 4096-bit RSA keys in about an hour.

side-04-c3.text: Joe Loughry, David A. Umphress (2002). Information Leakage from Optical Emanations. ACM Transactions on Information and System Security.
side-04-c3.quote: LED status indicators on data communication equipment, under certain conditions, are shown to carry a modulated optical signal that is significantly correlated with information being processed by the device.
side-04-c3.claim: Loughry and Umphress (2002) showed that LEDs on serial-port devices were often wired directly to the data line, transmitting every bit they handled.

side-04-c3.text: Mordechai Guri, Boris Zadov, Eran Atias, Yuval Elovici (2017). LED-it-GO: Leaking (a lot of) Data from Air-Gapped Computers via the (small) Hard Drive LED. arXiv.
side-04-c3.quote: We show that a malware can indirectly control the HDD LED, turning it on and off rapidly (up to 5800 blinks per second) - a rate that exceeds the visual perception capabilities of humans.
side-04-c3.claim: Guri's group (Ben-Gurion University) extended this to malware-controlled hard-drive activity LEDs as a covert exfiltration channel from air-gapped machines.

side-05-c1.text: (2018). Meltdown and Spectre. meltdownattack.com (Graz University of Technology).
side-05-c1.quote: CVE-2017-5754 is the official reference to Meltdown.
side-05-c1.claim: Meltdown (CVE-2017-5754, mainly Intel, plus some ARM and IBM cores) abused out-of-order execution to read kernel memory from a userspace process.

side-05-c1.text: (2018). Meltdown and Spectre. meltdownattack.com (Graz University of Technology).
side-05-c1.quote: CVE-2017-5753 and CVE-2017-5715 are the official references to Spectre.
side-05-c1.claim: Spectre (CVE-2017-5753 / 5715) is broader: train the branch predictor to mispredict, slip a speculative read of a victim secret through that mispredict, and exfiltrate via the same cache side channel.

side-05-c2.text: Yoongu Kim, Ross Daly, Jeremie Kim, Chris Fallin, Ji Hye Lee, Donghyuk Lee, Chris Wilkerson, Konrad Lai, Onur Mutlu (2014). Flipping Bits in Memory Without Accessing Them: An Experimental Study of DRAM Disturbance Errors. ACM/IEEE International Symposium on Computer Architecture (ISCA 2014).
side-05-c2.quote: By reading from the same address in DRAM, we show that it is possible to corrupt data in nearby addresses. More specifically, activating the same row in DRAM corrupts data in nearby rows.
side-05-c2.claim: As DRAM cells shrunk, they became electrically noisy: rapidly activating one DRAM row ("hammering") leaks charge to neighboring rows and can flip bits there.

side-05-c2.text: (2019). RAMBleed: Reading Bits in Memory Without Accessing Them. rambleed.com.
side-05-c2.quote: RAMBleed is a side-channel attack that enables an attacker to read out physical memory belonging to other processes.
side-05-c2.claim: RAMBleed (2019) flipped the model again: instead of writing, it reads bits, a row's flip propensity reveals the value in adjacent rows, making RowHammer into a memory-disclosure side channel.

side-05-c3.quote: Hertzbleed takes advantage of our experiments showing that, under certain circumstances, the dynamic frequency scaling of modern x86 processors depends on the data being processed.
side-05-c3.claim: Hertzbleed (Wang et al., USENIX Security 2022) opened a new channel: dynamic frequency scaling.

side-05-c3.quote: We have demonstrated how a clever attacker can use a novel chosen-ciphertext attack against SIKE to perform full key extraction via remote timing, despite SIKE being implemented as “constant time”.
side-05-c3.claim: Hertzbleed used this to extract SIKE post-quantum key-agreement secrets via remote timing: work the SIKE designers had specifically engineered to be constant-time at the instruction level.

side-04-c1.text: Markus G. Kuhn (2003). Compromising emanations: eavesdropping risks of computer displays (UCAM-CL-TR-577). University of Cambridge, Computer Laboratory.
side-04-c1.quote: The civilian computer-security community became aware of the risk through the work of van Eck in 1985.
side-04-c1.claim: strong enough that, in 1985, Dutch researcher Wim van Eck publicly demonstrated reconstructing the displayed image from a van parked outside the building, using off-the-shelf TV equipment.

side-04-c1.text: Markus G. Kuhn (2003). Compromising emanations: eavesdropping risks of computer displays (UCAM-CL-TR-577). University of Cambridge, Computer Laboratory.
side-04-c1.quote: This report documents eavesdropping experiments on contemporary computer displays. It discusses the nature and properties of compromising emanations for both cathode-ray tube and liquid-crystal monitors.
side-04-c1.claim: Markus Kuhn's PhD work (2003) showed that LCDs and video cables leak reconstructable EM signatures (keyboards were shown to leak too, by Vuagnoux and Pasini in 2009).
